claim: When the head tilts laterally, eyes counterrotate less than 20%.
source: When your head tilts laterally, as in sports, reaching, and resting, your eyes counterrotate less than 20%, and thus eye images rotate, over a total range of about 180°.
evidence: Cited in the abstract as a known phenomenon

claim: When the head tilts laterally, eye images rotate over a total range of about 180°.
source: When your head tilts laterally, as in sports, reaching, and resting, your eyes counterrotate less than 20%, and thus eye images rotate, over a total range of about 180°.
evidence: Stated as a consequence of limited counterrotation

claim: Despite retinal image rotation during head tilt, the world appears stable and vision remains normal.
source: Yet, the world appears stable and vision remains normal.
evidence: Stated as an observed perceptual phenomenon

claim: Among IT neurons with consistent object orientation tuning, 63% remained stable with respect to gravity across tilts.
source: Among IT neurons with consistent object orientation tuning, 63% remained stable with respect to gravity across tilts.
evidence: Quantitative result from the study's neural recordings

claim: Gravitational tuning in IT neurons depends on vestibular/somatosensory cues.
source: Gravitational tuning depended on vestibular/somatosensory but also visual cues, consistent with previous evidence that IT processes scene cues for gravity's orientation.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the experiments

claim: Gravitational tuning in IT neurons depends on visual cues.
source: Gravitational tuning depended on vestibular/somatosensory but also visual cues, consistent with previous evidence that IT processes scene cues for gravity's orientation.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the experiments

claim: IT processes scene cues for gravity's orientation.
source: Gravitational tuning depended on vestibular/somatosensory but also visual cues, consistent with previous evidence that IT processes scene cues for gravity's orientation.
evidence: Referenced as previous evidence

claim: An internal gravitational reference frame is important for physical understanding of object position, posture, structure, shape, movement, and behavior.
source: In addition to stability across image rotations, an internal gravitational reference frame is important for physical understanding of a world where object position, posture, structure, shape, movement, and behavior interact critically with gravity.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the functional significance

claim: Eyes compensate less than 20% for lateral head tilt during sports.
source: Reflexive eye movements compensate for up/down and right/left head movements, but when your head tilts laterally, as during sports, driving (Zikovitz and Harris, 1999), social communication (Halberstadt and Saitta, 1987; Mignault and Chaudhuri, 2003; Krumhuber et al., 2007; Mara and Appel, 2015), working in cramped environments, reaching for distant objects, and resting in bed, your eyes compensate less than 20% (Miller, 1962; Schworm et al., 2002), so retinal images rotate around the point of fixation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Eyes compensate less than 20% for lateral head tilt during driving.
source: Reflexive eye movements compensate for up/down and right/left head movements, but when your head tilts laterally, as during sports, driving (Zikovitz and Harris, 1999), social communication (Halberstadt and Saitta, 1987; Mignault and Chaudhuri, 2003; Krumhuber et al., 2007; Mara and Appel, 2015), working in cramped environments, reaching for distant objects, and resting in bed, your eyes compensate less than 20% (Miller, 1962; Schworm et al., 2002), so retinal images rotate around the point of fixation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Retinal images rotate around the point of fixation during lateral head tilt.
source: Reflexive eye movements compensate for up/down and right/left head movements, but when your head tilts laterally, as during sports, driving (Zikovitz and Harris, 1999), social communication (Halberstadt and Saitta, 1987; Mignault and Chaudhuri, 2003; Krumhuber et al., 2007; Mara and Appel, 2015), working in cramped environments, reaching for distant objects, and resting in bed, your eyes compensate less than 20% (Miller, 1962; Schworm et al., 2002), so retinal images rotate around the point of fixation.
evidence: Stated as a consequence of incomplete compensation

claim: Perceptual compensation for retinal image rotation is automatic and complete.
source: But the perceptual compensation for this is so automatic and complete that we are usually unaware of the image rotation, and visual abilities are not strongly affected.
evidence: Stated as an observed perceptual phenomenon

claim: Our perceptual reference frame for objects remains stable with respect to the environment and gravity during head tilt.
source: Critically, our perceptual reference frame for objects remains stable with respect to the environment and gravity.
evidence: Stated as a key perceptual phenomenon

claim: The primate ventral visual pathway implements an object-centered reference frame.
source: Our previous work has shown that the primate ventral visual pathway (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991) implements an object-centered reference frame (Pasupathy and Connor, 1999; Pasupathy and Connor, 2001; Pasupathy and Connor, 2002; Carlson et al., 2011; Srinath et al., 2021; Brincat and Connor, 2004; Brincat and Connor, 2006; Yamane et al., 2008; Hung et al., 2012; Connor and Knierim, 2017), stabilizing against position and size changes on the retina.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: The ventral visual pathway stabilizes object representation against position and size changes on the retina.
source: Our previous work has shown that the primate ventral visual pathway (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991) implements an object-centered reference frame (Pasupathy and Connor, 1999; Pasupathy and Connor, 2001; Pasupathy and Connor, 2002; Carlson et al., 2011; Srinath et al., 2021; Brincat and Connor, 2004; Brincat and Connor, 2006; Yamane et al., 2008; Hung et al., 2012; Connor and Knierim, 2017), stabilizing against position and size changes on the retina.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: One channel in anterior ventral pathway processes scene-level visual cues for the orientation of the gravitational reference frame.
source: Our recent work has shown that one channel in anterior ventral pathway processes scene-level visual cues for the orientation of the gravitational reference frame (Vaziri et al., 2014; Vaziri and Connor, 2016), raising the possibility that the ventral pathway reference frame is aligned with gravity.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work

claim: The ventral pathway reference frame is aligned with gravity.
source: Here, we confirmed this hypothesis in anterior IT (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991), and found that gravitational alignment depends on both visual and vestibular/somatosensory (Brandt et al., 1994; Baier et al., 2012) cues.
evidence: Stated as a confirmed hypothesis from the current study

claim: Gravitational alignment in anterior IT depends on both visual and vestibular/somatosensory cues.
source: Here, we confirmed this hypothesis in anterior IT (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991), and found that gravitational alignment depends on both visual and vestibular/somatosensory (Brandt et al., 1994; Baier et al., 2012) cues.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Object orientation in either reference frame (gravitational or retinal) is linearly decodable from IT population responses with high accuracy.
source: To a lesser extent, we observed tuning aligned with the retinal reference frame, and object orientation in either reference frame was linearly decodable from IT population responses with high accuracy.
evidence: Stated as a finding from decoding analysis

claim: Humans have voluntary perceptual access to either gravitational or retinal reference frame.
source: This is consistent with psychophysical results showing voluntary perceptual access to either reference frame (Attneave and Reid, 1968).
evidence: Supported by citation to psychophysical study

claim: The dominant gravitationally aligned reference frame confers stability across image rotations.
source: The dominant, gravitationally aligned reference frame not only confers stability across image rotations but also enables physical understanding of objects in a world dominated by the force of gravity.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of functional significance

claim: The dominant gravitationally aligned reference frame enables physical understanding of objects in a world dominated by gravity.
source: The dominant, gravitationally aligned reference frame not only confers stability across image rotations but also enables physical understanding of objects in a world dominated by the force of gravity.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of functional significance

claim: Compensatory ocular counter-rolling was measured to be 6° based on iris landmarks.
source: Compensatory ocular counter-rolling was measured to be 6° based on iris landmarks visible in high-resolution photographs, consistent with previous measurements in humans (Miller, 1962; Schworm et al., 2002) and larger than previous measurements in monkeys (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014), making it unlikely that we failed to adequately account for the effects of counterroll.
evidence: Stated as a measurement from the study

claim: The measured 6° ocular counter-rolling is consistent with previous measurements in humans.
source: Compensatory ocular counter-rolling was measured to be 6° based on iris landmarks visible in high-resolution photographs, consistent with previous measurements in humans (Miller, 1962; Schworm et al., 2002) and larger than previous measurements in monkeys (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014), making it unlikely that we failed to adequately account for the effects of counterroll.
evidence: Comparison with cited previous studies

claim: The measured 6° ocular counter-rolling is larger than previous measurements in monkeys.
source: Compensatory ocular counter-rolling was measured to be 6° based on iris landmarks visible in high-resolution photographs, consistent with previous measurements in humans (Miller, 1962; Schworm et al., 2002) and larger than previous measurements in monkeys (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014), making it unlikely that we failed to adequately account for the effects of counterroll.
evidence: Comparison with cited previous studies

claim: Eye rotation would need to be five times greater than previously observed to mimic gravitational tuning.
source: Eye rotation would need to be five times greater than previously observed to mimic gravitational tuning.
evidence: Stated as a calculation to rule out alternative explanation

claim: Maximum correspondence for retinally-tuned neurons was observed at a compensation value of 6°.
source: The fact that maximum correspondence, for those neurons tuned in the retinal reference frame, was observed at a compensation value of 6° (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicates that counterrotation during the experiments was consistent with our measurements outside the experiments.
evidence: Stated as a finding from analysis shown in figure supplement

claim: For the example neuron in Figure 1, object orientation tuning remained consistent with respect to gravity across the two tilt conditions with full scene stimuli.
source: For this neuron, object orientation tuning remained consistent with respect to gravity across the two tilt conditions, with a peak response centered at 0° (dashed vertical line).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1c,d

claim: For the example neuron in Figure 1, the correlation between the two curves in gravitational coordinates is 0.99.
source: The correlation between the two curves in gravitational coordinates is 0.99 (t=25.89, p=3.28 X 10–8).
evidence: Quantitative statistical result from the data

claim: For the example neuron in Figure 1, object information has been transformed into the gravitational reference frame.
source: Thus, the object information signaled by this neuron, which necessarily originates in retinal coordinates, has been transformed into the gravitational reference frame.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the correlation result

claim: Of the 52 neurons with consistent object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames, 63% (33/52) were aligned with gravity.
source: Of the 52 neurons with consistent object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames, 63% (33/52) were aligned with gravity, 21% (11/52) were aligned with the retinae, and 15% (8/52) were aligned with both.
evidence: Quantitative result from population analysis

claim: Of the 52 neurons with consistent object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames, 21% (11/52) were aligned with the retinae.
source: Of the 52 neurons with consistent object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames, 63% (33/52) were aligned with gravity, 21% (11/52) were aligned with the retinae, and 15% (8/52) were aligned with both.
evidence: Quantitative result from population analysis

claim: Of the 52 neurons with consistent object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames, 15% (8/52) were aligned with both gravitational and retinal reference frames.
source: Of the 52 neurons with consistent object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames, 63% (33/52) were aligned with gravity, 21% (11/52) were aligned with the retinae, and 15% (8/52) were aligned with both.
evidence: Quantitative result from population analysis

claim: The population tendency toward positive correlation was strongly significant along the gravitational axis (p=6.49 X 10–29).
source: The population tendency toward positive correlation was strongly significant along the gravitational axis (two-tailed randomization t-test for center-of-mass relative to 0; p=6.49 X 10–29) and also significant though less so along the retinal axis (p=5.76 X 10–10).
evidence: Statistical test result from population analysis

claim: The population tendency toward positive correlation was significant along the retinal axis (p=5.76 X 10–10).
source: The population tendency toward positive correlation was strongly significant along the gravitational axis (two-tailed randomization t-test for center-of-mass relative to 0; p=6.49 X 10–29) and also significant though less so along the retinal axis (p=5.76 X 10–10).
evidence: Statistical test result from population analysis

claim: For isolated object stimuli, 60% of the 53 neurons with significant object orientation tuning (32/53) showed significant correlation in the gravitational reference frame.
source: In this case, 60% of the 53 neurons with significant object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames (32/53) showed significant correlation in the gravitational reference frame, 26% (14/53) significant correlation in the retinal reference frame, and within these groups 13% (7/53) were significant in both reference frames.
evidence: Quantitative result from isolated object condition

claim: For isolated object stimuli, 26% of the 53 neurons with significant object orientation tuning (14/53) showed significant correlation in the retinal reference frame.
source: In this case, 60% of the 53 neurons with significant object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames (32/53) showed significant correlation in the gravitational reference frame, 26% (14/53) significant correlation in the retinal reference frame, and within these groups 13% (7/53) were significant in both reference frames.
evidence: Quantitative result from isolated object condition

claim: For isolated object stimuli, 13% of the 53 neurons with significant object orientation tuning (7/53) were significant in both reference frames.
source: In this case, 60% of the 53 neurons with significant object orientation tuning in one or both reference frames (32/53) showed significant correlation in the gravitational reference frame, 26% (14/53) significant correlation in the retinal reference frame, and within these groups 13% (7/53) were significant in both reference frames.
evidence: Quantitative result from isolated object condition

claim: For isolated object stimuli, the population tendency toward positive correlation was significant along the gravitational axis (p=3.63 X 10–22).
source: The population tendency toward positive correlation was again significant in this experiment along both gravitational (p=3.63 X 10–22) and retinal axes (p=1.63 X 10–7).
evidence: Statistical test result from isolated object condition

claim: For isolated object stimuli, the population tendency toward positive correlation was significant along the retinal axis (p=1.63 X 10–7).
source: The population tendency toward positive correlation was again significant in this experiment along both gravitational (p=3.63 X 10–22) and retinal axes (p=1.63 X 10–7).
evidence: Statistical test result from isolated object condition

claim: Gravitational tuning can depend primarily on vestibular/somatosensory cues for self-orientation.
source: This suggests that gravitational tuning can depend primarily on vestibular/somatosensory cues for self-orientation.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the isolated object results

claim: Gravitational tuning did not depend on the horizon or ground surface in the background condition.
source: Nonetheless, the Figure 2b result confirms that gravitational tuning did not depend on the horizon or ground surface in the background condition.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the isolated object results

claim: The accuracy of linear discriminant models for orientation match/non-match in the gravitational reference frame was 97%.
source: The accuracy of these linear models for orientation match/non-match in the gravitational reference frame was 97% (10-fold cross-validation).
evidence: Quantitative result from decoding analysis

claim: The accuracy of linear discriminant models for orientation match/non-match in the retinal reference frame was 98%.
source: The accuracy of models for orientation match/non-match in the retinal reference frame was 98%.
evidence: Quantitative result from decoding analysis

claim: For isolated object stimuli, the accuracy of linear discriminant models for orientation match/non-match in the gravitational reference frame was 81%.
source: (The accuracies for analyses based on the partially overlapping population of 99 neurons tested with isolated objects were 81% gravitational and 90% retinal.)
evidence: Quantitative result from decoding analysis

claim: For isolated object stimuli, the accuracy of linear discriminant models for orientation match/non-match in the retinal reference frame was 90%.
source: (The accuracies for analyses based on the partially overlapping population of 99 neurons tested with isolated objects were 81% gravitational and 90% retinal.)
evidence: Quantitative result from decoding analysis

claim: Information in both gravitational and retinal reference frames is easily decodable as weighted sums across the neural population.
source: The success of these simple linear models shows that information in both reference frames was easily decodable as weighted sums across the neural population.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the decoding results

claim: Linear decoding of information in both reference frames is consistent with psychophysical results showing that humans have voluntary access to either reference frame.
source: This easy, linear decoding of information in both reference frames is consistent with psychophysical results showing that humans have voluntary access to either reference frame (Attneave and Reid, 1968).
evidence: Comparison with cited psychophysical study

claim: High decoding accuracy was obtained with models based solely on neurons that showed no significant correlation in either gravitational or retinal reference frames: 89% for gravitational discrimination and 97% for retinal discrimination.
source: High accuracy was obtained even with models based solely on neurons that showed no significant correlation in either gravitational or retinal reference frames (Figure 2a, light gray): 89% for gravitational discrimination and 97% for retinal discrimination.
evidence: Quantitative result from decoding analysis on subset of neurons

claim: Neurons with no significant correlation in either reference frame carry a mix of retinal and gravitational object orientation signals.
source: This supports the idea that these neurons carry a mix of retinal and gravitational object orientation signals.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the decoding results

claim: In the cue conflict experiment, 54% (67/123) of neurons with significant correlation showed object orientation tuning aligned with the retinal reference frame.
source: Of these, 54% (67/123) showed object orientation tuning aligned with the retinal reference frame, 35% (43/123) with the gravitational reference frame, and 11% (13/123) with both (Figure 4a).
evidence: Quantitative result from cue conflict experiment

claim: In the cue conflict experiment, 35% (43/123) of neurons with significant correlation showed object orientation tuning aligned with the gravitational reference frame.
source: Of these, 54% (67/123) showed object orientation tuning aligned with the retinal reference frame, 35% (43/123) with the gravitational reference frame, and 11% (13/123) with both (Figure 4a).
evidence: Quantitative result from cue conflict experiment

claim: In the cue conflict experiment, 11% (13/123) of neurons with significant correlation showed object orientation tuning aligned with both reference frames.
source: Of these, 54% (67/123) showed object orientation tuning aligned with the retinal reference frame, 35% (43/123) with the gravitational reference frame, and 11% (13/123) with both (Figure 4a).
evidence: Quantitative result from cue conflict experiment

claim: In the cue conflict experiment, the population tendency toward retina-aligned orientation tuning was significant (p=8.14 X 10–28).
source: The population tendency toward retina-aligned orientation tuning was significant (two-tailed randomization t-test for center-of-mass relative to 0; p=8.14 X 10–28) as was the tendency toward gravity-aligned orientation tuning (p=6.23 X 10–6).
evidence: Statistical test result from cue conflict experiment

claim: In the cue conflict experiment, the population tendency toward gravity-aligned orientation tuning was significant (p=6.23 X 10–6).
source: The population tendency toward retina-aligned orientation tuning was significant (two-tailed randomization t-test for center-of-mass relative to 0; p=8.14 X 10–28) as was the tendency toward gravity-aligned orientation tuning (p=6.23 X 10–6).
evidence: Statistical test result from cue conflict experiment

claim: Visual cues contribute to gravity-aligned tuning under normal circumstances where they combine with convergent vestibular/somatosensory cues.
source: The main result in this experiment, that many IT neurons exhibit object orientation tuning aligned with visual cues for the direction of gravity, even in the presence of conflicting vestibular/somatosensory cues, argues that visual cues contribute to gravity-aligned tuning under normal circumstances, where they combine with convergent vestibular/somatosensory cues.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the cue conflict results

claim: Many neurons in IT are strongly tuned for the orientation of large-scale ground surfaces and edges.
source: That would be consistent with our previous discovery that many neurons in IT are strongly tuned for the orientation of large-scale ground surfaces and edges, in the orientation ranges experienced across head tilts (Brincat and Connor, 2004; Brincat and Connor, 2006), and more generally with the strong visual representation of scene information in temporal lobe (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Epstein, 2008; Lescroart and Gallant, 2019; Kornblith et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: There is strong visual representation of scene information in temporal lobe.
source: That would be consistent with our previous discovery that many neurons in IT are strongly tuned for the orientation of large-scale ground surfaces and edges, in the orientation ranges experienced across head tilts (Brincat and Connor, 2004; Brincat and Connor, 2006), and more generally with the strong visual representation of scene information in temporal lobe (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Epstein, 2008; Lescroart and Gallant, 2019; Kornblith et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: The gravitational reference frame remains stable across retinal image rotations.
source: The gravitational reference frame remains stable across retinal image rotations, a critical advantage for vision from the tilting platform of the head and body.
evidence: Stated as a functional advantage

claim: The gravitational reference frame enables understanding of object structure, posture, shape, motion, and behavior relative to gravity.
source: And, it enables understanding of object structure, posture, shape, motion, and behavior relative to the strong gravitational force that constrains and interacts with all these factors.
evidence: Stated as a functional advantage

claim: The average rotational invariance in IT is ~90° for in-plane rotation.
source: There is a degree of rotational invariance in IT, but even by the broadest definition of invariance (angular range across which responses to an optimal stimulus remain significantly greater than average responses to random stimuli) the average is ~90° for in-plane rotation and less for out-of-plane rotations (Hung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The average rotational invariance in IT is less than 90° for out-of-plane rotations.
source: There is a degree of rotational invariance in IT, but even by the broadest definition of invariance (angular range across which responses to an optimal stimulus remain significantly greater than average responses to random stimuli) the average is ~90° for in-plane rotation and less for out-of-plane rotations (Hung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Spatial position information is transformed from retinal coordinates into relative spatial relationships between parts of contours, surfaces, object parts, and objects.
source: In particular, spatial position information is transformed from retinal coordinates into relative spatial relationships between parts of contours, surfaces, object parts, and objects (Connor and Knierim, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Orientation information is transformed from the reference frame of the eyes to the gravitational reference frame.
source: Our results here indicate a novel kind of transformation of orientation information in the ventral pathway, from the original reference frame of the eyes to the gravitational reference frame that defines physical interactions in the world.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study

claim: The representation of orientation with respect to gravity is invariant to changes in the observer system, especially lateral head tilt.
source: Because this is an allocentric reference frame, the representation of orientation with respect to gravity is invariant to changes in the observer system (especially lateral head tilt), making representation more stable and more relevant to external physical events.
evidence: Stated as a consequence of the allocentric reference frame

claim: Rosenberg and Angelaki (2014) reported significant alignment with eye orientation for 45 of 92 (49%) tilt tests in CIP neurons.
source: Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014 measured the responses of 46 CIP neurons with two monkey tilts, right and left 30°, and fit the responses with linear models. They reported significant alignment with eye orientation for 45 of 92 (49%) tilt tests (two separate tests for each neuron, right and left), intermediate between eye and gravity for 26/92 tilt tests (28%), and alignment with gravity for 6/92 tilt tests (7%).
evidence: Cited result from previous study

claim: Rosenberg and Angelaki (2014) reported intermediate alignment between eye and gravity for 26/92 (28%) tilt tests in CIP neurons.
source: Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014 measured the responses of 46 CIP neurons with two monkey tilts, right and left 30°, and fit the responses with linear models. They reported significant alignment with eye orientation for 45 of 92 (49%) tilt tests (two separate tests for each neuron, right and left), intermediate between eye and gravity for 26/92 tilt tests (28%), and alignment with gravity for 6/92 tilt tests (7%).
evidence: Cited result from previous study

claim: Rosenberg and Angelaki (2014) reported alignment with gravity for 6/92 (7%) tilt tests in CIP neurons.
source: Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014 measured the responses of 46 CIP neurons with two monkey tilts, right and left 30°, and fit the responses with linear models. They reported significant alignment with eye orientation for 45 of 92 (49%) tilt tests (two separate tests for each neuron, right and left), intermediate between eye and gravity for 26/92 tilt tests (28%), and alignment with gravity for 6/92 tilt tests (7%).
evidence: Cited result from previous study

claim: Only one CIP neuron in Rosenberg and Angelaki (2014) appeared to show significant alignment with gravity for both tilt directions.
source: However, of the 5 neurons in this last category, only one appeared to show significant alignment with gravity for both tilt directions (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014; Figure 4D).
evidence: Cited result from previous study

claim: Orientation tuning of ~35% of CIP neurons was sensitive to monkey tilt.
source: Thus, while orientation tuning of ~35% of CIP neurons was sensitive to monkey tilt and gravity-aligned information could be extracted with a neural network (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014), there was no explicit tuning in a gravitational reference frame or dominance of gravitational information as found here.
evidence: Cited result from previous study

claim: Gravity-aligned information could be extracted from CIP neurons with a neural network.
source: Thus, while orientation tuning of ~35% of CIP neurons was sensitive to monkey tilt and gravity-aligned information could be extracted with a neural network (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014), there was no explicit tuning in a gravitational reference frame or dominance of gravitational information as found here.
evidence: Cited result from previous study

claim: There was no explicit tuning in a gravitational reference frame or dominance of gravitational information in CIP as found in IT.
source: Thus, while orientation tuning of ~35% of CIP neurons was sensitive to monkey tilt and gravity-aligned information could be extracted with a neural network (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014), there was no explicit tuning in a gravitational reference frame or dominance of gravitational information as found here.
evidence: Comparison between cited study and current results

claim: Parietal and frontal cortex are deeply involved in perceiving and predicting physical events.
source: There is however compelling human fMRI evidence that parietal and frontal cortex are deeply involved in perceiving and predicting physical events (Fischer et al., 2016), and have unique abstract signals for stability not detected in ventral pathway (Pramod et al., 2022), though these could reflect decision-making processes (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Parietal and frontal cortex have unique abstract signals for stability not detected in ventral pathway.
source: There is however compelling human fMRI evidence that parietal and frontal cortex are deeply involved in perceiving and predicting physical events (Fischer et al., 2016), and have unique abstract signals for stability not detected in ventral pathway (Pramod et al., 2022), though these could reflect decision-making processes (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Ventral pathway object and scene processing may be a critical source of information about gravity and its effects on objects.
source: Our results and others (Gallivan et al., 2014; Gallivan et al., 2016; Cesanek et al., 2021) suggest nonetheless that ventral pathway object and scene processing may be a critical source of information about gravity and its effects on objects, especially when detailed object representations are needed to assess precise shape, structure, support, strength, flexibility, compressibility, brittleness, specific gravity, mass distribution, and mechanical features to understand real world physical situations.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation supported by current and cited work

claim: Mental rotation of shapes is time consuming in proportion to the angle of required rotation.
source: Humans can perform tasks requiring mental rotation of shapes, but this is time consuming in proportion to the angle of required rotation (Shepard and Metzler, 1971), and seems to rely on an unusual strategy of covert motor simulation (Wexler et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Mental rotation seems to rely on an unusual strategy of covert motor simulation.
source: Humans can perform tasks requiring mental rotation of shapes, but this is time consuming in proportion to the angle of required rotation (Shepard and Metzler, 1971), and seems to rely on an unusual strategy of covert motor simulation (Wexler et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The rotation required for gravitational reference frame transformation is fast and automatic.
source: The rotation required here is fast and so automatic as to be unnoticeable.
evidence: Stated as a contrast to mental rotation

claim: Two head-restrained male rhesus monkeys were trained to maintain fixation within 1° of a 0.3° diameter spot for 4 s to obtain a juice reward.
source: Two head-restrained male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were trained to maintain fixation within 1° (radius) of a 0.3° diameter spot for 4 s to obtain a juice reward.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Image stimuli were displayed on a 3840x2160 resolution, 80.11 DPI television screen.
source: Image stimuli were displayed on a 3840x2160 resolution, 80.11 DPI television screen placed directly in front of the monkey, centered at eye level at a distance of 60 cm.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The screen subtended 70° vertically and 100° horizontally.
source: The screen subtended 70° vertically and 100° horizontally.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Monkeys were seated in a primate chair attached to a +/–25° full-body rotation mechanism.
source: Monkeys were seated in a primate chair attached to a+/–25° full-body rotation mechanism with the center of rotation at the midpoint between the eyes, so that the angle of gaze toward the fixation point remained constant across rotations.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The center of rotation was at the midpoint between the eyes, so that the angle of gaze toward the fixation point remained constant across rotations.
source: Monkeys were seated in a primate chair attached to a+/–25° full-body rotation mechanism with the center of rotation at the midpoint between the eyes, so that the angle of gaze toward the fixation point remained constant across rotations.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: After fixation was initiated, 4 stimuli were presented sequentially, for 750ms each, separated by 250ms intervals with a blank, gray background.
source: After fixation was initiated by the monkey, 4 stimuli were presented sequentially, for 750ms each, separated by 250ms intervals with a blank, gray background.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: All stimuli in a given generation were tested in random order for a total of five repetitions.
source: All stimuli in a given generation were tested in random order for a total of five repetitions.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Recording positions ranged from 5 to 25 mm anterior to the external auditory meatus within the inferior temporal lobe.
source: Recording positions ranged from 5 to 25 mm anterior to the external auditory meatus within the inferior temporal lobe, including the ventral bank of the superior temporal sulcus, lateral convexity, and basal surface.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: A total of 368 object-selective IT neurons were studied with different combinations of experiments.
source: A total of 368 object-selective IT neurons were studied with different combinations of experiments.
evidence: Description of experimental sample size

claim: All animal procedures were approved by the Johns Hopkins Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol # PR21M442).
source: All animal procedures were approved by the Johns Hopkins Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol # PR21M442) and conformed to US National Institutes of Heath and US Department of Agriculture guidelines.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: Response rates for each stimulus were calculated by counting action potentials during the presentation window and averaging across five repetitions.
source: Response rates for each stimulus were calculated by counting action potentials during the presentation window and averaging across five repetitions.
evidence: Description of data analysis methods

claim: Orientation tuning functions were smoothed with boxcar averaging across three neighboring values.
source: Orientation tuning functions were smoothed with boxcar averaging across three neighboring values.
evidence: Description of data analysis methods

claim: Significance of positive correlations were measured with a one-tailed randomization t-test, p=0.05.
